questions.question: A Cambodian province retrains its malaria-spraying model monthly; its dashboard shows drift and district error rates, but no reading triggers action, as the team relies on retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner set a threshold and response for each indicator
options.B: Send the dashboard to the board each month for its review
options.C: Have the IS auditor set alert thresholds for each indicator
options.D: Rely on monthly retraining to correct drift as it builds up

questions.key_concept: AI monitoring indicators need owner-set thresholds within approved tolerance and a defined response when breached.
questions.pre_read: Ask what reading would make someone act, and what they would then do.
questions.correct_explanation: Indicators without thresholds tell no one when to act, so drift or district error rates can worsen while everyone watches. The model owner should set thresholds inside the tolerance senior management approved, each tied to a response such as review, retraining through change control or disengagement. Sending the dashboard to the board raises visibility, but without thresholds the board has no basis for deciding when a reading needs action.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because board reporting shows seriousness. But raw readings with no thresholds give the board no trigger for action either.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is objective. But setting thresholds is the owner's decision within approved tolerance; the IS auditor assesses them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining refreshes the model. But scheduled retraining measures nothing and can learn from drifted or bad data; it does not replace thresholds that trigger review.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor set operating thresholds that the owner sets, and D trusts scheduled retraining that measures nothing.
Final two: A beats B because the owner, within approved tolerance, decides when a reading needs action and what follows; raw readings sent to the board trigger nothing.
Exam cue: a key risk indicator needs a threshold and a response; a dashboard of numbers with neither is monitoring in name only.

questions.question: An Iraqi freight platform's carrier-vetting model rejects 30% of trucking firms' applications; its monitoring tracks cargo theft only among carriers it approved. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have shippers report theft by approved carriers within a week
options.B: Lower the model's threshold so it rejects fewer trucking firms
options.C: Have experts review a sample of the rejected firms
options.D: Compare the 30% rejection rate with other freight platforms' rates

questions.key_concept: Monitoring that observes outcomes only for approved cases cannot see wrongful rejections; the screened-out population needs its own checks.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose outcomes the monitoring can ever observe, and whose it never can.
questions.correct_explanation: The model's outcomes are observed only for carriers it let through, so an honest firm wrongly turned away never produces a record showing the model was wrong, and monitoring can look healthy while wrongful rejections go unseen. Having experts review a sample of the rejected firms gives the screened-out population its own check. Faster theft reports, option A, are the runner-up: they speed the signal, but only for approved carriers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because lagging outcomes slow monitoring. But faster reports still cover approved carriers only; rejected applicants never produce an outcome to report.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fewer rejections sound fairer. But nothing yet shows the rejections are wrong; changing the threshold before checking them is guesswork.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because peer rates give context. But another platform's rejection rate says nothing about whether these rejections were wrong.

tips: Eliminate: B changes the threshold before anyone knows the rejections are wrong, and D compares rates that cannot show whether any rejection was wrong.
Final two: C beats A because faster theft reports still cover approved carriers only; rejected applicants need their own check.
Exam cue: when outcomes are seen only for cases a model approves, look for a separate check on the cases it screens out.

questions.question: An Indonesian motorcycle-finance company's chatbot, presented as a staff member named Sari, decides whether borrowers get extensions on loan repayments. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a supervisor review a weekly sample of borrowers' extension cases
options.B: Have Sari explain each extension decision in more detail
options.C: Post a general notice telling borrowers the company uses AI
options.D: Tell borrowers an AI system decides and how to reach a person

questions.key_concept: People affected by an AI decision must be told AI was involved and how to reach a person who can review and change it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a borrower believes about who decided, and what they could do if they disagreed.
questions.correct_explanation: Borrowers who think a staff member named Sari decided their extension have no reason to ask for human review, and no route to one. Telling them that an AI system makes the decision, and how to reach a staff member who can change it, gives affected people the means to challenge it. A weekly supervisor sample adds oversight, but borrowers still cannot see that a machine decided or seek review of their own case.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling adds oversight. But it reviews a few cases after the fact; borrowers still do not know an AI decided or how to challenge it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reasons help borrowers. But reasons from an apparent staff member hide that an AI decided, and still give no route to a person.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it discloses AI use. But a general notice does not tell each borrower their own decision was automated or how to seek review.

tips: Eliminate: B adds reasons while borrowers still think a person decided, and C gives a general notice that does not reach each decision.
Final two: D beats A because sampling oversees some decisions, but only disclosure and a route to a person let each borrower challenge their own.
Exam cue: affected people can challenge an AI decision only if they know an AI was involved and how to reach someone who can change it.

questions.question: A Paraguayan power cooperative's discount-tariff eligibility model logs the factors behind each decision, yet every rejected applicant gets the same three 'main reasons', whatever their application showed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check the three reasons against the model's top global features
options.B: Give applicants the specific reasons for their own cases
options.C: Stop sending reasons, since generic ones may mislead applicants
options.D: Refer applicants to the model's vendor for case explanations

questions.key_concept: Explanations to affected people must be local: specific to their own decision and traceable to the log, not the model's global feature importance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the explanation would differ between two applicants with different applications.
questions.correct_explanation: Identical reasons for everyone explain nothing about any one rejection, so applicants cannot tell what to challenge or correct. Each applicant should get the reasons recorded for their own decision, drawn from the decision log, so an appeal can address their actual application. Confirming the three reasons match the model's top global features shows what drives the model overall, but a global explanation still cannot say which factors decided one case.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it checks the reasons are real model drivers. But global feature importance describes the model overall, not which factors decided one applicant's case.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because misleading reasons cause harm. But no reasons leave applicants less able to challenge; the fix is accurate reasons, not none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the cooperative owns its decisions and must explain them; a vendor has no duty to applicants.

tips: Eliminate: C removes reasons instead of correcting them, and D passes the cooperative's duty to explain its own decisions to a vendor.
Final two: B beats A because only local, case-specific reasons let an applicant challenge their own decision; global feature importance explains the model, not the case.
Exam cue: an explanation helps an affected person only if it is specific to their decision and traceable to the log.

questions.question: An Azerbaijani pipeline operator's corrosion model will choose which pipe sections get inspected; under 2% are corroded, and the draft acceptance criterion is 95% overall accuracy. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a cap on missed corroded sections, set from risk tolerance
options.B: Raise the overall accuracy pass mark from 95% to 99%
options.C: Require the model to flag at least 2% of pipe sections
options.D: Use the vendor's published accuracy figure as the criterion

questions.key_concept: When the outcome is rare, acceptance criteria must target the costly error, such as missed cases, not overall accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Ask which error would hurt most here, and whether the criterion measures that error at all.
questions.correct_explanation: With under 2% of sections corroded, a model that flags nothing scores over 98% accuracy, so the 95% criterion can pass a model that misses every corroded pipe. The error that matters is a missed corroded section, so the criterion should cap that rate, set from risk tolerance. Raising the bar to 99% still lets a model pass while missing half or more of the corroded sections.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a higher bar seems stricter. But with under 2% corroded, 99% accuracy can still miss half or more of them; the measure is the problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it matches the corrosion rate. But a model can flag 2% of sections and still pick mostly sound pipes; volume is not detection.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor figures are ready-made. But they are inputs, measured on other data, and still an overall figure.

tips: Eliminate: C sets a flagging quota that says nothing about which pipes are found, and D borrows an overall figure measured on someone else's data.
Final two: A beats B because with rare corrosion, overall accuracy stays high while corroded sections are missed; only a cap on misses measures that error.
Exam cue: when the event is rare, overall accuracy flatters; set criteria on the costly error, such as missed cases.

questions.question: A Cameroonian parliament's clerks approved a debate summarizer after each read about 20 outputs, keeping no record of inputs or results; the vendor updates the model monthly. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: About 20 outputs per clerk is too small a test sample
options.B: The clerks may lack the technical skill to test an AI model
options.C: No fixed test cases exist to rerun after each model change
options.D: The tool was not tested on the vendor's standard benchmark

questions.key_concept: Approval of a generative AI tool needs recorded test cases and results; unrecorded spot reads give no baseline for the approval or for later updates.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the parliament could rerun next month to see whether the tool got worse.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative output varies and the vendor changes the model monthly, so the parliament needs a fixed, recorded set of test cases with expected qualities that can be rerun after each update. Without one, nothing shows how the tool performed or whether an update made it worse. Twenty outputs per clerk may also be too few, but even a larger informal read would leave nothing to rerun.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small samples are weak. But a larger unrecorded read would still leave nothing to compare after each monthly update.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI testing can be technical. But clerks who know the debates are the right judges of summary accuracy; domain expertise is what this test needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks are standardized. But a vendor benchmark measures general ability, not accurate summaries of these debates.

tips: Eliminate: B doubts the domain experts best placed to judge summaries, and D swaps the parliament's own use for a general benchmark.
Final two: C beats A because a bigger informal sample still cannot be rerun; a recorded test set lets each monthly update be checked.
Exam cue: for generative AI that changes often, look for a documented, rerunnable test set; unrecorded spot reads give no baseline.

questions.question: A Greek mobile operator's SIM-swap fraud model flags men and women, and younger and older customers, at similar rates, yet women aged over 70 file most complaints. Which result should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: Wrongful-flag rates for women and for those aged over 70, separately
options.B: Overall accuracy on recent confirmed fraud cases
options.C: The vendor's fairness benchmark for SIM-swap fraud detection
options.D: Wrongful-flag rates for combined groups such as older women

questions.key_concept: Fairness by single attributes can hide gaps in combined groups, such as older women; test the intersections that the evidence points to.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether groups tested one attribute at a time could hide a smaller group where they overlap.
questions.correct_explanation: Similar flag rates by sex and by age can hide a gap where the two meet: a model can treat women, and older customers, fairly on average while wrongly flagging older women far more often. The complaints point to that combined group, so wrongful-flag rates for intersections such as older women can confirm or rule out the gap. Wrongful-flag rates by sex and by age alone still average older women in with everyone else.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it counts wrongful flags for both complaining groups. But each rate alone averages over older women, so the gap stays hidden.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy on confirmed cases matters. But an overall figure says nothing about how any one group is treated, least of all a small combined group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because benchmarks are ready-made. But a vendor benchmark uses other operators' data and customers; it cannot show how this operator's older female customers are treated.

tips: Eliminate: B gives one overall figure, and C borrows a benchmark built on other operators' data and customers.
Final two: D beats A because gaps can sit where groups combine; rates for each attribute alone average them away.
Exam cue: fair results for each attribute alone do not prove fairness for combined groups; test the intersections the evidence points to.

questions.question: A Maltese health service's fall-risk model misses falls among wheelchair users no more often than among others, but the test held 25 wheelchair users among 40,000 patients. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The model treats wheelchair users as fairly as other patients
options.B: The test is too small to show reliably how wheelchair users fare
options.C: The model is likely biased and needs retraining on more wheelchair users
options.D: The overall miss rate across 40,000 patients settles the question

questions.key_concept: Group fairness results need enough cases per group; with very few, the right conclusion is that fairness is not yet shown.
questions.pre_read: Count how many people the group result rests on before reading the rate.
questions.correct_explanation: With only 25 wheelchair users, one or two extra missed falls would change their rate sharply, so matching the average proves little either way. The sound conclusion is that the test cannot yet show how these patients fare; a larger, targeted sample is needed before anyone concludes the model is fair or unfair. Calling it biased and retraining assumes a problem the evidence has not shown.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the rates match. But 25 people are too few for the match to mean much; the result could easily differ in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small groups are often underserved. But the evidence does not show bias; it shows the test cannot tell either way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 40,000 is large. But an overall rate is dominated by other patients and can hide how a small group fares.

tips: Eliminate: A reads a match on 25 people as proof, and D lets 40,000 other patients stand in for a small group.
Final two: B beats C because the evidence is too thin to show bias either way; concluding the model is biased goes beyond it.
Exam cue: check group sizes before trusting group results; a tiny group's rate supports no conclusion, good or bad.

questions.question: A Cypriot sports-betting regulator's validators received only the builders' summary metrics for a new match-fixing alert model; their requests for its data and code were refused. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Give validators the data and code access that challenge requires
options.B: Have validators recompute the builders' summary metrics for errors
options.C: Have the IS auditor review the code in the validators' place
options.D: Accept the builders' summary, as their tests cover the same ground

questions.key_concept: Independent validation needs access to the model's data, code and design; validators limited to builders' summaries cannot challenge the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the validators could actually examine, not only who they report to.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent validation means challenging the model, its data, design and code, not checking the builders' arithmetic. Without access, validators can only restate what the builders chose to report, so the validation is independent in name only. Recomputing the summary metrics confirms the sums but not whether the data, labels or method behind them are sound, which is where weaknesses in an alert model usually hide.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recomputation is a real check. But it confirms the builders' arithmetic, not the data, labels or design behind the numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But validation is a management control; the IS auditor assesses it and does not perform it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because builders test their work. But builders' testing is never independent validation; their summary is what needs challenge.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the IS auditor perform validation, and D treats the builders' own testing as independent validation.
Final two: A beats B because effective challenge needs the data and code; recomputing a summary only checks the builders' arithmetic.
Exam cue: independent validators need access as well as independence; without data and code, validation only restates the builders' report.

questions.question: An Armenian robo-advice firm's investment assistant was red-teamed only by security engineers, who tested data theft and system-prompt leaks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before launch?

options.A: Have the security engineers add jailbreak attempts to their tests
options.B: Rely on the vendor's filter to block harmful replies to customers
options.C: Have the IS auditor red-team the assistant before it launches
options.D: Add unsuitable-product scenarios, judged by financial planners

questions.key_concept: Red teaming covers harmful outputs to the system's own users, judged by domain specialists, not only data theft by attackers.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the assistant could hurt the customers who use it exactly as intended.
questions.correct_explanation: Security engineers test whether attackers can steal data, but for an investment assistant a likely harm is advice that is wrong or unsuitable for the customer, such as pushing risky products on a retiree. Red teaming should include those harmful-output scenarios, judged by specialists who know what suitable advice looks like. Adding jailbreak attempts widens the security tests, but engineers would still not judge whether fluent advice suits the customer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because jailbreaks can unlock harmful replies. But security engineers would still judge attacks, not whether polite, fluent advice suits the customer.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters block harmful text. But a filter tuned for offensive content will not spot advice that is polite, fluent and unsuitable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But red teaming is a test the owner commissions; the IS auditor assesses its scope and results.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a content filter to judge suitability, and C makes the IS auditor perform testing that the owner commissions.
Final two: D beats A because more attack types still leave unsuitable advice unjudged; financial planners must judge what customers are told.
Exam cue: red teaming covers how a system can harm its own users, judged by people who know the domain, not only attacks by outsiders.

questions.question: A Lao forestry department's illegal-logging model retrains weekly on villagers' app photos, using the labels villagers choose themselves. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Rival groups copying the model by querying it repeatedly
options.B: Altered photos fooling the model at the moment they are scored
options.C: Mislabeled photos teaching the model to miss illegal logging
options.D: Mass uploads of labeled photos slowing the app for others

questions.key_concept: When untrusted users supply training data or labels for regular retraining, poisoning is the leading threat.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can influence what the model learns, not only what it scores.
questions.correct_explanation: Because villagers choose the labels and the model retrains on them every week, anyone with the app can shape what it learns: people profiting from logging could label clear-cut sites as normal forest until the model stops flagging them. That is data poisoning, and it changes the model for every future decision. Altered photos that fool the model at scoring time succeed one decision at a time; they do not change the model itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because extraction is a known threat. But nothing suggests open scoring access, and a copied logging model offers little gain.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because evasion is common. But it fools one decision at a time; open labels feeding weekly retraining change the model itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because uploads are open. But slow service is an availability issue; it does not corrupt what the model learns.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes open scoring access the stem never describes, and D slows the service without changing what the model learns.
Final two: C beats B because labels feeding retraining change the model for everyone; evasion fools single decisions.
Exam cue: when untrusted users supply training labels, poisoning is the first threat to weigh.

questions.question: A Senegalese recipe site's chatbot allows users 30 prompts an hour; overnight, a few accounts filled their quotas with pasted whole cookbooks, exhausting the monthly model budget. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the model usage budget agreed with the vendor
options.B: Cap prompt length and daily token use per account, with alerts
options.C: Lower each user's limit from 30 prompts an hour to 10
options.D: Block the accounts involved and keep the current prompt limits

questions.key_concept: Public AI services need per-user token and input-size limits, because model cost follows tokens and attackers can exhaust it: a denial of AI service.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one user could cost the service, and what stops them.
questions.correct_explanation: Model cost grows with the tokens in each prompt, so a count of prompts does not bound spending: a few accounts sent huge prompts within their quota and exhausted the budget, a denial of AI service. Capping prompt length and token use per account, with alerts on unusual use, bounds what any user can consume. A lower hourly prompt limit cuts the number of prompts, not their size.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more budget restores service. But it raises the cost of the next attack without preventing it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tighter limits slow abuse. But cost follows tokens, not prompt count; ten whole cookbooks an hour still drain the budget.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it stops the source. But new accounts are easy to open, and the limits that allowed the attack stay unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: A pays for the attack instead of preventing it, and D blocks these accounts while leaving the gap open for new ones.
Final two: B beats C because model cost follows prompt size; a lower prompt count still lets each prompt carry a whole book.
Exam cue: for public generative AI, limit tokens and input size, not only request counts; compute is what attackers exhaust.

questions.question: A Ukrainian grain trader's pricing assistant reads market news websites; it passed prompt-injection tests in which testers typed attacks into its chat window. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retest it with attack instructions hidden in news web pages
options.B: Rely on the chat tests, since the same model reads both sources
options.C: Block websites from unfamiliar domains at the network firewall
options.D: Filter injected instructions out of the assistant's final answers

questions.key_concept: Direct injection tests do not cover indirect injection through content an assistant reads; each input path needs its own tests.
questions.pre_read: List every source of text the assistant reads, then ask which of them the tests used.
questions.correct_explanation: Reading websites opens a path for indirect prompt injection: anyone who can publish a page, comment or ad can plant instructions the assistant may follow. Typed chat attacks test only the direct path, so they say little about this one. Retesting with instructions hidden in web pages shows what the assistant does with them. Blocking unfamiliar domains narrows exposure, but trusted news sites can carry injected text too.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one model handles both. But indirect injection arrives inside content the assistant treats as data; the chat tests never tried that path.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it limits sources. But familiar sites can host injected comments or ads, and a firewall cannot read instructions in content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filters catch some attacks. But injected instructions can act through the assistant's tools or shape answers without appearing in them.

tips: Eliminate: B treats typed chat tests as covering web content, and D filters answers, which misses instructions acting through tools.
Final two: A beats C because only testing shows how the assistant handles injected web content; blocking domains narrows exposure, but trusted sites can carry injections.
Exam cue: direct and indirect injection are different paths; test every source of text the assistant reads, not only its chat window.

questions.question: An Austrian ski resort's public guest chatbot answers from an internal wiki that all 900 seasonal staff can edit. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Limit the chatbot's admin console to two named engineers
options.B: Place the chatbot behind a web application firewall
options.C: Let only named, reviewed authors change its source pages
options.D: Add an output filter that blocks offensive words in its replies

questions.key_concept: In retrieval-based assistants, anyone who can edit source content can inject instructions, so write access to sources is an AI control.
questions.pre_read: List who can put text in front of the model, including through its sources.
questions.correct_explanation: Every page the chatbot retrieves is text it may treat as instructions, so any of 900 seasonal staff could plant content that steers what guests are told: an indirect prompt injection from inside. Restricting edits of the chatbot's source pages to named authors, with review, controls that path. Locking down the chatbot's admin console protects its settings but leaves the wiki content, where this risk sits, open to every editor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because admin access is privileged. But the open path is the wiki text the chatbot retrieves, which 900 staff can still edit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because firewalls protect web apps. But injected text arrives as ordinary content through allowed channels; a firewall cannot judge instructions in it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because offensive replies are visible harm. But injected instructions can mislead guests with polite, false answers that a word filter passes.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a firewall that cannot read instructions in content, and D blocks rude words while polite, misleading answers pass.
Final two: C beats A because the chatbot takes its answers from wiki text; locking the admin console leaves that path open to 900 editors.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based assistants, whoever can write the source content can steer the answers; control who writes it.

questions.question: A South Korean comics platform's translation service loads whichever model its registry tags 'production'; code releases need approval, and 60 data scientists have registry write access. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log every production tag move for review each month
options.B: Encrypt the registry's stored model files at rest
options.C: Confirm that every code release to the translation service is approved
options.D: Let only the approved release process move the production tag

questions.key_concept: A model registry tag can deploy a model without any code release, so only the approved release process may move it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually decides which model runs in production, and who can change it.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving the tag swaps the translation model without any code release, so in practice the tag is the deployment and registry write access is the power to deploy. With 60 people able to move it, a mistaken or deliberate switch reaches production untested and unapproved. Letting only the approved release process move the tag brings model deployment under change control. Monthly log review finds a harmful switch weeks after it went live.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs create accountability. But review a month later finds a harmful switch after its translations have reached readers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects stored files. But it does not limit who can move the production tag, which is what deploys a model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because code change control is the usual release gate. But moving the tag swaps the model with no code release, so approved code releases never cover it.

tips: Eliminate: B protects stored files but not who can move the tag, and C checks code releases that a tag move bypasses.
Final two: D beats A because restricting who moves the tag prevents untested switches; monthly log review finds them after they act.
Exam cue: in MLOps, a registry tag or alias can be a deployment; whoever can move it can change production AI.

questions.question: An Emirati co-working operator's facilities agent reads supplier emails and, 'to be useful', can order repairs, unlock members' doors and edit contracts at any time. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to ask staff before unlocking doors
options.B: Grant task-scoped rights and require approval for high-impact actions
options.C: Remove the agent's door-unlocking right as its highest-risk permission
options.D: Limit who can send requests to the agent to facility managers

questions.key_concept: AI agents get task-scoped rights and system-enforced approval for high-impact actions; usefulness does not justify broad standing permissions.
questions.pre_read: List what the agent's account could do right now if something steered it wrongly.
questions.correct_explanation: Rights the agent always holds mean anything that steers it, such as an instruction hidden in a supplier email or a plain mistake, can unlock members' doors, order repairs or rewrite contracts at once. Scoping rights to each task and requiring a person's approval, enforced by the systems, for high-impact actions bounds the damage. Removing the door right first looks risk-based but leaves repairs and contracts open to the same steering.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But prompt instructions can be overridden by injected text or errors; permissions hold where instructions do not.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because removing the riskiest right first looks risk-based. But the agent could still order repairs and edit contracts on injected or mistaken instructions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it narrows access. But the agent also acts on supplier emails, so injected text can still steer it; the agent's own rights are what need bounding.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction that injected text can override, and D limits who can message the agent while injected emails still reach it.
Final two: B beats C because removing one right leaves repairs and contracts open; every right needs scoping, with approval for high-impact actions.
Exam cue: 'more useful' is no reason for standing rights; judge an agent by what its account can do, not what it is told.

questions.question: A Montenegrin tax office's AI vendor warned an update may put plausible wrong amounts in tax notices, raising no errors; procurement left it unread for nine days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send vendor AI notices to incident intake with named triage roles
options.B: Have procurement check the inbox daily and forward any urgent mail
options.C: Treat vendor notices as change requests for the next release
options.D: Require the vendor to fix flaws before releasing any update

questions.key_concept: Vendor notices about model flaws are AI incident signals and must flow into incident intake with named triage roles.
questions.pre_read: Trace the path a vendor's warning takes before anyone acts on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor warning that its model may misstate tax amounts is an AI incident signal: households may already be receiving wrong notices. Because such errors look normal and trip no alarms, outside signals like vendor notices may be the only early warning. They belong in the incident process, with named roles to triage them by impact on the people affected. Daily inbox checks by procurement still depend on someone spotting the right email.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because faster reading shortens the delay. But procurement cannot judge AI impact, and forwarding still depends on someone recognizing an incident.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the fix will come as a vendor update. But wrong notices may already be reaching households; a release-cycle request delays triage of harm happening now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors should test releases. But no contract ends model flaws; this warning arrived and failed only because nobody who could act read it.

tips: Eliminate: C files a live harm as a routine change for later, and D asks for flawless releases instead of fixing how warnings are handled.
Final two: A beats B because incident intake brings named triage by impact; a faster inbox check still depends on procurement spotting the risk.
Exam cue: vendor notices, complaints and red-team findings are AI incident detection channels; check that they reach triage.

questions.question: A Czech poison-information center rates AI incidents by users affected and downtime, so a chatbot telling 12 callers a cleaning-product mix was safe was rated low. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise this incident to high and keep the current rating scale
options.B: Rate AI incidents by how many model outputs were affected
options.C: Add severity of harm to people to the AI incident rating scale
options.D: Have the IS auditor rate the severity of each AI incident

questions.key_concept: AI incident severity must weigh harm to people, not just user counts or downtime; a scale without it misrates harmful errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the rating scale measures, and whether a single serious harm could ever score high.
questions.correct_explanation: Wrongly telling 12 callers that a chemical mix was safe could injure them, yet a scale built on user counts and downtime rates it low. The scale itself is the gap: AI incidents must be triaged by the severity of harm to people as well as by scale and business impact. Re-rating this incident fixes one case, but the next harmful answer with few users or no downtime would be misrated again.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because this incident is clearly underrated. But fixing one rating leaves the scale that misrated it in place for the next incident.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it measures spread. But output counts are another volume measure; they still miss how badly each person could be harmed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor is objective. But rating incidents is the incident team's operating task; the IS auditor assesses the method.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one volume measure for another, and D gives the IS auditor an operating task that belongs to the incident team.
Final two: C beats A because the scale caused the misrating; re-rating one incident leaves the next one exposed.
Exam cue: AI incident triage weighs harm to people, not just users affected or downtime; check the rating scale itself.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Kill switch readiness
questions.question: An Egyptian irrigation authority's canal-gate model has a tested kill switch to its previous version, its only fallback, which reads the same sensor feeds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test the kill switch each month as well as before go-live
options.B: Obtain a vendor attestation that both versions tolerate feed faults
options.C: Rely on the previous model version as the fallback
options.D: Prepare and rehearse a manual way to operate the gates

questions.key_concept: Disengagement needs a rehearsed fallback that does not depend on the model or its feeds; an older version on the same inputs can fail alike.
questions.pre_read: Ask what takes over when the model is switched off, and whether it shares the model's weak points.
questions.correct_explanation: The kill switch hands the gates to the previous version, which reads the same sensor feeds, so a feed fault or a shared flaw would leave no safe way to run them. A rehearsed manual procedure is a fallback that depends on no model, which makes disengagement a real option. Relying on the previous version, option C, is the runner-up: the handover is tested, but that version fails whenever the shared feeds do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tested switches are reliable. But a switch that hands control to a version on the same feeds still leaves no fallback if both fail.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a vendor attestation sounds like assurance. But it is a claim, not a fallback; if the shared feeds fail, nothing safe takes over the gates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an earlier version is a known state. But it reads the same feeds, so one feed fault or shared flaw stops both; a manual fallback does not.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps testing a switch without asking what takes over, and B relies on a vendor's claim instead of a working fallback.
Final two: D beats C because the previous version shares the same feeds and may fail with them; only a manual fallback works when the models cannot be trusted.
Exam cue: disengaging an AI system needs a rehearsed fallback for its work that does not depend on the same model or feeds.

questions.question: A Malawian tobacco auction rolled back its bale-grading model after two days of wrong grades that set growers' pay; grading is now normal, but those payments stand uncorrected. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Close the incident, since grading has now returned to normal
options.B: Use decision logs to find and regrade the affected bales
options.C: Retrain the model on the affected bales' corrected grades
options.D: Start root cause analysis on the faulty model version

questions.key_concept: Containment is not the end: decision logs identify the people affected during the faulty period so their harm can be remedied.
questions.pre_read: Ask who was affected before the rollback, and how the auction would find them.
questions.correct_explanation: Rolling back stopped new wrong grades, but bales graded during those two days still carry wrong grades, and growers may already have been paid on them. The decision logs show which bales the faulty version graded, so they can be regraded and growers' payments corrected. Root cause analysis must follow, but it fixes the model for the future; it does nothing for growers already harmed by wrong grades.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an ordinary incident closes once service is confirmed. But service is not fully restored while grades from the faulty days still set growers' pay.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses corrected data. But it is an untested change made before the cause is known, and it does not fix grades already issued.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause prevents recurrence. But it serves future sales; growers already harmed need their grades corrected first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats normal new grades as full recovery, though wrong grades from the faulty days still set pay, and C makes an untested change before the cause is known.
Final two: B beats D because bales already carry wrong grades that growers are paid on; finding and remedying them comes before diagnosing the model.
Exam cue: after containment, use decision logs to identify the people affected and remedy their harm.

questions.question: A Uruguayan wool mill's output-forecast model began over-forecasting when a new truck scale arrived, whose readings for similar loads are 2.2 times the old scale's. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Correct the truck scale feed's units through change control
options.B: Retrain the model on recent data including the truck scale readings
options.C: Roll back to the previous model version until it is fixed
options.D: Widen the forecast alert threshold to absorb the larger readings

questions.key_concept: Root cause analysis for AI traces failures across data, model, prompt and integration layers; fix the layer that failed, through change control.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed in the inputs when the problem began, before deciding what to fix.
questions.correct_explanation: A jump of about 2.2 times for similar loads is the pounds-to-kilograms ratio, so the cause sits in the integration layer: the new scale's feed sends the wrong units. The model is behaving as designed on wrong inputs, so the fix belongs in the feed through change control. Rolling back to an earlier model changes nothing, since that version would receive the same inflated weights; retraining would teach the model to treat pounds as normal.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining adapts the model. But it would learn from mislabeled units, hiding the fault and breaking forecasts again once the feed is fixed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rollback is a standard containment step. But the model did not change; an older version fed the same wrong units fails the same way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the larger readings now trip forecast alerts. But widening the threshold hides a real error from monitoring instead of correcting it.

tips: Eliminate: B teaches the model to accept wrong units, and D widens the alert threshold, so monitoring stops flagging a real input fault.
Final two: A beats C because the cause is in the feed; rolling back a model that did not change leaves the wrong units flowing.
Exam cue: trace an AI failure across layers (data, model, prompt, integration) before choosing a fix; the model is not always the cause.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Closing problem records
questions.question: A Guyanese water utility's voice bot failed Creolese-speaking callers three times as often as others; a retrained version passed release tests, and the problem record was closed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the record closed, since the retrained version passed its tests
options.B: Add a notice that the bot may misunderstand some ways of speaking
options.C: Reopen the record until production results show the gap has closed
options.D: Have the IS auditor retest the retrained voice bot before closing

questions.key_concept: AI problem records close only when production evidence shows the fix removed the harm, not when a retrained version passes release tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence shows callers are now understood, and when it was gathered.
questions.correct_explanation: A problem record closes when the cause is removed and the fix is shown to work. Release tests show the retrained version met its criteria before go-live, not that Creolese-speaking callers now get through. Keeping the record open until production results by language show the gap has closed gives that proof. Closing on release tests alone could leave the gap in place, unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tests passed. But release tests show the version met its criteria; only production results show Creolese-speaking callers now get through.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns callers. But a notice treats the symptom; Creolese speakers would still be failed by the bot.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But verifying a fix is management's task; the IS auditor assesses whether it was done.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a notice while callers are still failed, and D gives the IS auditor verification work that management owns.
Final two: C beats A because release tests do not prove the harm stopped; production results by group show whether the fix worked.
Exam cue: close an AI problem record only when evidence from production shows the fix worked for the people affected.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Linked pages in a retrieval index
questions.question: A Togolese agriculture ministry's crop-advice assistant answers farmers from an index of approved websites plus any page those sites link to, which no one vets. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Scan every indexed page for hidden instructions before each answer
options.B: Show farmers the source link with every answer given
options.C: Have an owner approve each page, linked ones too, before indexing
options.D: Add a disclaimer that farmers should verify the advice

questions.key_concept: Retrieval sources are AI data: each needs an owner who approves its origin and fitness before it enters the index, including pages added automatically.
questions.pre_read: Ask how a page gets into the assistant's index and who checks it first.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieved pages are data the assistant turns into advice, so each page needs an owner who has checked its origin and fitness. Pages linked from approved sites enter the index unchecked and can be wrong, outdated or planted. Owner approval of every page, linked ones included, before indexing closes that gap. Scanning for hidden instructions catches one attack, but not inaccurate or outdated advice from a page nobody checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because planted instructions are a real retrieval threat. But a scan finds only injection, not wrong or outdated advice from pages nobody checked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sources help farmers judge answers. But a link leaves the check to farmers after the advice is given, and unchecked pages still shape it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns farmers. But a disclaimer shifts the check to farmers and leaves unchecked pages feeding the advice.

tips: Eliminate: B and D both leave the check to farmers after the advice is given; the control belongs before content enters the index.
Final two: C beats A because retrieval sources need owner-checked provenance; a scan for hidden instructions misses pages that are simply wrong or out of date.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based assistants, ask who approved each source in the index, including anything added automatically.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A supplier's data recall
questions.question: A data vendor says 4% of the harvest records it sold a Sri Lankan coconut exporter were wrong; nine of the exporter's models may have trained on them. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Use lineage records to find model versions trained on those records
options.B: Retrain the nine models on the vendor's corrected records
options.C: Ask the vendor to warrant the accuracy of future deliveries
options.D: Monitor the nine models for accuracy drops over the next month

questions.key_concept: Lineage links each model version to its training data, so a data defect can be traced to the models it affected before anyone retrains.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the exporter would know which models learned from the wrong records.
questions.correct_explanation: Lineage records tie each model version to the data snapshots it learned from, so they show which of the nine models used the wrong records, and how many. That impact analysis tells model owners which models need retesting or retraining, and in what order. Retraining all nine at once is an untested change made before anyone knows which models were affected or whether their outputs harmed decisions.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because corrected data is available. But it retrains models that may be unaffected, untested, before lineage shows which versions used the wrong records.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the source. But a warranty is a vendor claim about future data; it does nothing for models already trained.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring catches decline. But a small share of wrong records may never show as a visible accuracy drop, and decisions rest on them meanwhile.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a vendor warranty, a claim that cannot fix models already trained, and D waits for an accuracy drop that bad records may never cause.
Final two: A beats B because lineage shows which model versions learned from the wrong records; retraining all nine first is untested and may be needless.
Exam cue: when training data turns out to be wrong, trace it through lineage to every model version it reached before acting.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Hauls removed by a cleaning rule
questions.question: A Mauritanian fishing fleet's catch-forecast model was trained after a cleaning rule deleted every haul over five tons as a sensor fault; trawlers land most such hauls. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain on twice as many hauls, cleaned by the same rule
options.B: Have the data owner fix the rule and restore real hauls
options.C: Raise trawlers' forecasts by a fixed correction factor
options.D: Test the model's trawler forecasts separately before release

questions.key_concept: Cleaning rules shape what a model learns: deleting real extreme cases as errors leaves the model unable to forecast them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the records a cleaning rule removed were errors or real events.
questions.correct_explanation: The rule treated real trawler hauls as sensor faults, so the model never learned what large catches look like and will forecast them too low. Having the data owner fix the rule and restore the real hauls repairs the data the model learns from. Testing trawler forecasts separately would expose the gap, but the training data would still lack the hauls that cause it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But the same rule would delete the large hauls again; volume cannot restore what cleaning removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it offsets low forecasts. But a fixed factor guesses at the error and leaves the model trained on incomplete data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing by group reveals gaps. But it would only confirm this one; the deleted hauls would still be missing from training.

tips: Eliminate: A adds hauls that the same rule would strip out again, and C patches forecasts with a guessed factor instead of fixing the data.
Final two: B beats D because the gap comes from real hauls the rule deleted; a separate trawler test would confirm it but leave the data incomplete.
Exam cue: when a cleaning rule removes outliers, ask whether they were errors or real cases the model must learn.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Filling blank weight fields
questions.question: A Kiribati health service's diabetes-risk model fills blank weight fields with the national average weight; most blanks belong to outer-island patients whose clinics have no scales. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The weight field may breach the service's completeness standard
options.B: The national average weight may be several years out of date
options.C: Staff may overwrite outer-island patients' weights without approval
options.D: The model may misjudge outer-island patients as a group

questions.key_concept: Missing data that clusters in one group, filled with a single value, gives the model a systematic error for that group.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the blanks belong to and what the model will learn about them.
questions.correct_explanation: Filling blanks with the national average gives most outer-island patients a weight they may not have, so the model learns and applies a made-up figure to one group. Its errors for them will be systematic, not random, and can underestimate or overestimate their diabetes risk. A completeness breach is real, but filling the blanks hides it and understates the harm: skewed care decisions for a whole group.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missing values are a data quality issue. But the fill makes the field look complete; the greater concern is the systematic error it creates for outer-island patients.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stale figures cause errors. But any single average misstates these patients' weights, and the stem gives no sign the figure is old.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because unapproved edits are a control gap. But nothing in the stem suggests staff edit values; the filling rule itself creates the error.

tips: Eliminate: B blames the figure's age, though any single average misstates these patients, and C assumes unapproved staff edits that the stem never describes.
Final two: D beats A because the filled-in values hit one group systematically, skewing their risk scores; a completeness breach understates that harm, and the fill even hides it.
Exam cue: when missing data clusters in one group, ask how the fill-in rule changes the model's decisions for that group.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Rotated image copies
questions.question: A Papua New Guinean coffee exporter's bean-defect team made five rotated copies of every photo, then randomly split all photos into training and test sets. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Test photos may be rotated copies of ones the model trained on
options.B: Rotated photos may not look like beans on the sorting belt
options.C: Five copies of each photo may overload the training servers
options.D: A random split may leave too few defective beans to test with

questions.key_concept: Augment after splitting: copies made before the split put near-identical images in training and test sets, inflating reported performance.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each rotated copy ends up after the random split.
questions.correct_explanation: Copies made before the split land on both sides of it, so the model is tested on rotated versions of photos it already learned. Its test score then overstates how it will do on new beans. Augmentation belongs after the split, applied to training data only. Unrealistic rotations are a smaller concern: they may add little, but they do not inflate the reported score.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because augmented data should be realistic. But rotated bean photos are plausible, and the larger flaw is that copies now sit in both sets.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data volume has costs. But compute capacity does not make the test result misleading; the copies across both sets do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rare defects need enough test cases. But the stem gives no sign defects are rare; copies in both sets are the stated flaw.

tips: Eliminate: C is a capacity question, not a test-validity one, and D assumes defects are rare, which the stem never says.
Final two: A beats B because copies on both sides of the split inflate the test score; unrealistic rotations would only weaken training.
Exam cue: copies, crops or rotations of one record must all fall on the same side of the split; check where each copy lands.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Choosing implant sensor inputs
questions.question: A Liechtenstein dental-implant maker's data scientists picked the 20 sensor inputs most linked to confirmed defects using the whole dataset, then split it into training and test sets. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Twenty inputs may be too few to detect implant defects
options.B: The chosen inputs may be hard to explain to the quality engineers
options.C: Test records may have influenced which inputs were chosen
options.D: Inputs linked to past defects may miss new kinds of defect

questions.key_concept: Feature selection is part of training: done on the whole dataset before splitting, it leaks test information and inflates results.
questions.pre_read: Ask which records the team looked at when choosing the 20 inputs.
questions.correct_explanation: Choosing inputs on the whole dataset lets the test records shape the model before testing, so the test is no longer unseen and its results overstate performance on new implants. Selection, like any step that learns from data, must use training data only. Missing new kinds of defect is a real limit of any model trained on past cases, but it is not what makes this test evidence unreliable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because input count affects detection. But no number is right in itself; the flaw is that test data shaped which inputs were chosen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because engineers need reasons. But explainability concerns how results are used; it does not decide whether this test evidence can be trusted.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new defect types appear. But that limits any model trained on past cases; here the test itself was compromised before it ran.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the input count as the flaw, though no count is right in itself, and B raises explainability, which does not bear on whether the test is valid.
Final two: C beats D because selecting on the whole dataset makes this test evidence unreliable now; new defect types are a general limit of past data.
Exam cue: any step that learns from data, including choosing inputs, must happen after the split, on training data only.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Monitoring plan at the deployment gate
questions.question: A Belizean shrimp farm's feed-ration models pass validation each sprint, but its deployment gate never asks who will monitor each model, or against what limits. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the gate, since each model passes validation before release
options.B: Revalidate each model against its limits 30 days after release
options.C: Have the IS auditor monitor each model after release
options.D: Require an owned monitoring plan with limits to pass the gate

questions.key_concept: A deployment gate should require a monitoring plan with an owner and limits; a validation pass describes the model only at release.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gate checks about the model's life after release, not just at release.
questions.correct_explanation: A validation pass shows a model met its criteria on the day it was tested; water, feed and stock conditions keep changing, so it can drift soon after release. A deployment gate should pass a model only with a monitoring plan naming who watches it and the limits that trigger action. A 30-day revalidation adds one more snapshot, but drift that starts sooner would set rations unnoticed until then.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because validation is the main gate. But it describes the model at release; nothing then shows when drift starts setting wrong rations.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it checks again. But one later snapshot still leaves weeks of unwatched rations, and drift can start at any time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But monitoring is the owner's control; the IS auditor assesses it and would otherwise audit their own work.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a validation pass as lasting assurance, and C has the IS auditor run monitoring that the model owner must run.
Final two: D beats B because drift can start any day after release; a monitoring plan with limits keeps watching, while a 30-day revalidation is one more snapshot.
Exam cue: a deployment gate should ask how the model will be watched after release, by whom and against what limits, not only whether it passed validation.

questions.question: A Seychelles tourism board's validation report names training run 287 of 300, but the deployed visitor-forecast model's registry entry records only its code version. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The code may have changed since run 287 was trained
options.B: Nothing shows the deployed model is the run that was validated
options.C: Running 300 trials may have overfitted the model
options.D: The registry may let staff deploy any model without approval

questions.key_concept: Experiment tracking must link the deployed model to the exact run that was validated; one code version produces many different models.
questions.pre_read: Ask what identifies a trained model, beyond the code that trained it.
questions.correct_explanation: The same code trained with different settings or data yields a different model on every run, so a code version does not identify which of the 300 runs is deployed. Without the run identifier, nothing shows that the validated model is the one in use. Overfitting from many runs is possible, but the stem's gap is traceability: validation evidence that may describe some other model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because code changes alter models. But even unchanged code yields a different model on each run; the recorded code version cannot say which run is live.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because many trials can overfit. But the stem gives no sign runs were picked on test results; the stated gap is linking deployed and validated models.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because registries need access control. But nothing in the stem points to unapproved deployment; the gap is which run was deployed.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes the code changed, though identical code still gives a different model each run, and D raises access control the stem never questions.
Final two: B beats C because validation evidence counts only for the model it tested; nothing ties run 287 to the deployed model, while overfitting is speculation.
Exam cue: a model is identified by its run, data and settings, not its code version; check that the validated artifact is the deployed one.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. What a model card leaves out
questions.question: A Lesotho wool exporter's fleece-grading model card gives accuracy and intended use, but nothing records how the training fleeces were sampled, graded or cleaned. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a datasheet on how the training set was built and checked
options.B: Add accuracy results for each fleece type to the model card
options.C: Retrain the model on a newly sampled set of fleeces
options.D: Have buyers confirm the grades on a sample of bales

questions.key_concept: Model documentation includes the training data's sources, sampling, labeling and processing, so its fitness and representativeness can be judged and traced.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model card tells you about the data, rather than the model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model card describes the model; a datasheet-style record describes its data: where the fleeces came from, how they were sampled and graded, and what cleaning removed. Without it, no one can judge whether the training data represents the fleeces the model will grade, or trace a bad grade to its cause. More accuracy figures describe results, not whether the data behind them was fit.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because breakdowns reveal weak spots. But results cannot show how the data was gathered or graded; without that, gaps and label errors stay unexplained.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because new data seems cleaner. But a new sample would be just as undocumented; the gap is the record, not the data itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because buyers see outcomes. But checking grades after sale finds errors late and says nothing about how the training data was built.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains on new data that would be just as undocumented, and D checks grades after sale, which cannot show how the data was built.
Final two: A beats B because data documentation shows whether the training data fits the use; more accuracy figures describe results, not the data behind them.
Exam cue: model documentation covers the data too: sources, sampling, labeling and cleaning, recorded so the IS auditor can trace them.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Limits found in validation
questions.question: A Kosovar grid operator's drone model for spotting damaged insulators missed many faults in fog during validation, yet its draft model card claims it suits all weather. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model with more foggy-flight images before release
options.B: Add a general statement that results may vary by weather
options.C: Record the fog limit in the model card and the usage rules
options.D: Have the IS auditor rewrite the card before its release

questions.key_concept: Model documentation must state the limits validation found, specifically, so users know when not to rely on the model.
questions.pre_read: Compare what validation found with what the model card promises.
questions.correct_explanation: A model card tells users where the model can be trusted. Validation found it misses insulator faults in fog, so the card must say so, and usage rules must stop crews from relying on it in fog. Otherwise inspectors will trust a clean result from a foggy flight. Retraining may follow, as the owner's choice, but it needs fresh validation, and the card must still state the limits found.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the weakness. But retraining is the owner's choice and needs revalidation; meanwhile the card would still promise all weather.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns users. But a vague caveat hides the specific, tested limit, so crews still cannot tell when to distrust results.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor found the error. But editing the card is the owner's job; the IS auditor recommends and later checks the change.

tips: Eliminate: B replaces a tested limit with a vague caveat crews cannot act on, and D has the IS auditor editing documentation the owner is accountable for.
Final two: C beats A because the card contradicts validation now; retraining is the owner's option and needs its own validation.
Exam cue: limits found in validation belong in the model card and in usage rules, stated as specifically as the tests found them.

questions.question: A Tajik railway retired its driver-fatigue model last quarter, but each driver's roster record still shows the model's last fatigue score, which planners keep consulting. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the scores, since the model was validated when it made them
options.B: Take the old scores off planners' screens and archive them
options.C: Retrain the retired model so its scores stay current
options.D: Remind planners that a fatigue score is one input among several

questions.key_concept: Decommissioning covers a model's stored outputs: withdraw them from use and keep them as records, or the retired model still shapes decisions.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the model still influences decisions after its switch-off.
questions.correct_explanation: Retiring a model includes its outputs still in use. The last scores reflect drivers' patterns from months ago, and no one monitors or validates them now, so planners are relying on a retired model to judge fatigue. Taking them off planners' screens ends that use, and archiving keeps them as records for any later inquiry. That the model was validated when it made them does not make months-old scores fit for today's rosters.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the scores came from a validated model. But validation covered conditions then; with no one monitoring the retired model, old scores cannot be trusted for today's rosters.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because current scores seem better. But it reverses the retirement decision without the owner, and a retrained model needs validation first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is quick. But reminders rarely change habits; the retired model's scores would still shape rosters.

tips: Eliminate: C reverses a retirement decision and adds an unvalidated model, and D relies on a reminder while the scores stay on screen.
Final two: B beats A because the scores came from a model no one now monitors; validation at the time does not make them fit for today's rosters.
Exam cue: a retired model is not retired while its stored outputs still drive decisions; withdraw them from use and keep them as records.

questions.question: A Gambian football league retired its ticket-demand model, but the model's monthly retraining job still copies fans' purchase records, with contact details, into its training store. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Restrict the training store's access to the named data team
options.B: Keep the retraining job running in case the model returns
options.C: Delete the model's code and records along with the job
options.D: Stop the job and dispose of its copies under retention rules

questions.key_concept: Retiring a model includes its pipelines: retraining jobs and data feeds must stop, with collected copies handled by the retention schedule.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else ran for the model besides the model itself.
questions.correct_explanation: Retirement covers the whole pipeline, not just the model. The retraining job keeps copying fans' contact details for a model that no longer runs, so personal data is processed with no purpose. Stopping the job ends that, and disposing of the copies under the retention schedule handles what was gathered. Restricting access reduces exposure but leaves the needless collection running.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because access control limits exposure. But the job would keep copying fans' details for a retired model; the collection itself has no purpose.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because restoring could be easier. But keeping a job alive just in case means processing personal data with no current purpose.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is thorough. But a retired model's records may be needed for later questions; the job and the copies are the problem, not the records.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps processing personal data with no current purpose, and C deletes records that later questions about past decisions may need.
Final two: D beats A because the retired model needs no new data; restricting access to the store still lets the job collect it.
Exam cue: decommissioning covers pipelines, retraining jobs, keys and data copies, not only the model endpoint.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A chatbot given a booking tool
questions.question: An Eswatini driving school linked its approved lesson-advice chatbot to its booking system so it can book lessons; IT tested only that the link works. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat the link as an AI change and test the chatbot's bookings
options.B: Accept IT's link test, since the chatbot's model is unchanged
options.C: Rerun the chatbot's approval tests on its lesson answers
options.D: Ask the vendor to confirm its model can handle lesson bookings

questions.key_concept: Giving an AI system a new tool or action is an AI change: test how it uses the tool, even when the model is unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the chatbot can do now that it could not do when it was approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Linking the chatbot to bookings changes what it can do: it now acts, not just answers, so its earlier approval no longer covers it. The link needs change control, with tests of how the chatbot books, such as wrong dates, double bookings and requests that try to misuse it. IT's link test shows only that the connection works, not how the chatbot behaves with it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model itself is unchanged. But a new tool changes what the chatbot can do; a link test shows the connection works, not how the chatbot books.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it retests the approved behavior. But the old tests cover answers only; the new risk is in the bookings the chatbot can now make.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But the vendor never saw the school's booking link, and its assurance is a claim, not a test.

tips: Eliminate: C retests only the answers the chatbot was approved for, and D relies on a vendor claim about a link the vendor never saw.
Final two: A beats B because a new tool changes what the chatbot can do; a link test proves the connection, not how the chatbot uses it.
Exam cue: connecting an AI system to a new tool, data source or action is an AI change, even when the model itself is unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Adding to a retrieval index
questions.question: A Djiboutian telecom regulator's staff assistant answers licensing questions from a document index; on Friday an analyst added 4,000 published licensing decisions to it, logging no change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check the decisions for personal data before they stay indexed
options.B: Treat the decisions as content, not a change, as they are public
options.C: Handle index additions as changes, with tests before release
options.D: Tell staff to confirm answers that cite the new decisions

questions.key_concept: In retrieval-based assistants, the index is part of the system: adding or removing content is a change that needs testing before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the assistant's answers could differ after the new decisions arrive.
questions.correct_explanation: What a retrieval assistant answers depends on its index, so adding 4,000 decisions changes its behavior as surely as a code release: old decisions may now be retrieved ahead of current rules, or crowd out other documents. Index additions need change control, with tests that answers stay correct. A personal-data check is narrower, and these decisions are already published; it does not show the assistant still answers correctly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because indexed documents can hold personal data. But these are already published; the larger risk is answers drawing on past decisions instead of current rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because public documents seem harmless. But content an assistant retrieves shapes its answers, so adding it changes the system's behavior.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff can catch errors. But it shifts testing onto users after release and relies on them spotting wrong answers.

tips: Eliminate: B treats retrieval content as harmless text though it shapes every answer, and D moves testing onto staff after release.
Final two: C beats A because the addition changes what the assistant answers; a personal-data check covers one risk, not whether answers remain correct.
Exam cue: in retrieval-based AI, changing the indexed content is a change to the system; expect change control and regression tests.
